desc:
arr is a permutation of the integers 0..n-1. Cut it into some number of contiguous chunks, sort every chunk on its own, and glue the chunks back together in their original order. You want the glued result to be the fully sorted array [0, 1, ..., n-1].

Return the largest number of chunks for which this works.

Example: arr = [1, 0, 2, 3, 4] returns 4: chunks [1, 0], [2], [3], [4].
constraints: arr is a permutation of 0 .. arr.length - 1
hints: A cut after position i is allowed only if everything on its left belongs to the left part of the sorted array. Which values must be on the left?
After a cut at i (left part has i + 1 elements), the left part must contain exactly the values 0..i.
Because arr is a permutation, the left part {arr[0..i]} equals {0..i} exactly when the maximum of arr[0..i] equals i. Count such positions.
editorial: Sorting a chunk puts its values in order inside the chunk's own positions, so the final array is sorted only if each chunk, occupying positions l..r, contains exactly the values l..r. A cut after index i is therefore valid precisely when the first i + 1 elements are the values 0..i.

For a permutation, the first i + 1 elements are i + 1 distinct values from 0..n-1, so their maximum is at least i; it equals i exactly when they are 0..i. Scan with a running maximum and count the indices where max == i. Each such index ends a chunk, and since cutting at every valid place gives the most chunks, that count is the answer.
One pass: O(n) time, O(1) space. (When values repeat or are arbitrary, this no longer works; the harder version compares a prefix maximum with a suffix minimum.)
